subject: Consistent finishes across a commercial interior
hook: Reception desk in one oak, storage in another, handles from three suppliers. Here's how finishes drift.
ig:
Reception desk in one oak, storage in another, handles from three suppliers. Here's how finishes drift.

Most business premises aren't furnished in one go. A reception desk one year, staff storage the next, a meeting room later. Each piece looks fine on its own, but together they slowly stop matching.

The usual causes:

- Different suppliers using different board decors, even when both are called 'oak-effect'.
- Edging picked by colour name rather than matched to the board.
- Grain direction not planned, so wood-effect runs look patchy.
- Handles chosen piece by piece.
- No written record of what was used last time.

The fix is simple: a finish schedule. One document listing the board decor, edging and handle for every type of furniture in the building. It's the first thing we put together on a commercial job.

Planning a fit-out or adding to an existing one? Save this, then tap the link in bio to talk to us about commercial furniture.
fb:
Walk into most offices and you'll spot it: the reception desk, the storage and the meeting room table are all 'oak', but none of them quite match.

It happens because furniture gets added over the years from different places, each using slightly different boards, edging and handles. The fix is a simple finish schedule, so everything made for the building uses the same decor, edging and hardware.

We've laid out the five most common reasons finishes drift in this carousel. If your business is planning a refurb or adding furniture, it's worth a look.

on_asset: S1: Why office finishes stop matching | And how to keep them consistent | S2: Different suppliers, different boards — An 'oak-effect' from one maker isn't the same decor as another's. Ordering from one workshop keeps the board range consistent. | S3: Edging that doesn't match — Edges are a separate product from the board. They need choosing to match the decor, not just the colour name. | S4: Grain running every which way — On wood-effect boards, grain direction should be planned across doors and panels so a run reads as one piece. | S5: Handles chosen job by job — Pick one handle style and finish for the whole building, and write it down. | S6: No record for next time — A simple finish schedule, listing board decor, edging and handles, makes future additions far easier to match. | S7: One building, one look — Save this for your next fit-out.
